items.title: MPs to debate the petition on SEND legal rights on 30 November
items.summary: A Westminster Hall debate on the petition to keep the legal right to SEND support is scheduled for Monday 30 November, after the petition closed with more than 117,000 signatures. A minister will respond at the end, and campaigners are urging MPs to ask about plans to change EHCP rights and about scrutiny of the coming Education for All Bill.
items.why: Families who rely on an EHCP to secure communication support and therapy may want to follow what ministers say about future legal protections.

items.title: DfE issues a SEND improvement notice to Leeds City Council
items.summary: The Department for Education has formally required Leeds City Council to improve its SEND services after the June 2026 Ofsted and CQC area inspection found widespread and systemic failings. Leeds must set up an independently chaired improvement board and deliver plans covering timely EHC plans, waits for neurodevelopmental assessment, health provision across schools and work with parents, with DfE reviews at least every six months and a target to finish by October 2027.
items.why: Families in Leeds waiting for an EHC plan or an assessment, including for pre-verbal and non-verbal children, should see progress tracked against these requirements and reported back to the DfE.

items.title: Bradford proposes 50 more special school places at a new satellite site in Bingley
items.summary: Bradford Council has proposed expanding Chellow Heights Special School from 260 to 310 pupils by opening a satellite site at Trinity All Saints CE Primary School in Bingley. The council says the number of local children with EHCPs has risen by more than 150% since 2019, and a public consultation runs until 4 December with a decision expected in January 2027.
items.why: Families in Bradford, including those of pre-verbal and non-verbal children who need a specialist place, can comment on the plans until 4 December.

items.title: Only one in six area SEND inspections this year has a positive outcome
items.summary: A Tes analysis of the 29 area SEND inspection reports published by Ofsted and the CQC in 2026 found that five areas received the most positive outcome, 20 were judged to give children inconsistent experiences and four, including Leeds, had widespread or systemic failings. Concerns about the content or delivery of EHC plans appeared in all but two of the reports.
items.why: When EHC plans are not delivered, agreed therapy or communication support may not reach children, and Leeds is the Yorkshire area found to have the most serious weaknesses.

items.title: DfE consults on draft guidance for children not in school registers
items.summary: The Department for Education has published draft statutory guidance on how council registers of children not in school will work, including which children are included and what information must be recorded. It also asks for views on piloting mandatory meetings before a child can be taken out of school to be home educated, and the consultation closes on 3 February 2027.
items.why: Families who home educate a pre-verbal or non-verbal child, or are considering it, can see what councils will record and respond before February.

items.title: Education Secretary says SEND bill and consultation response will arrive together, now expected in early 2027
items.summary: Lucy Powell told the Education Committee that the government will publish its SEND consultation response, National Inclusion Standards and an updated approach to Specialist Provision Packages alongside an Education for All Bill, which is now expected in early 2027. She did not say whether proposals affecting existing SEND rights would change, telling MPs they would need to wait for the bill.
items.why: Until the bill is published, families and therapists cannot see how future plans will set out communication support such as therapy or AAC, and current EHCP rights continue to apply.

items.title: Speech and language therapy workforce survey finds most services short of staff
items.source: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists
items.summary: The RCSLT's annual survey of 132 speech and language therapy services in England found 63% said their staffing was not enough to meet demand, rising to 74% of NHS services, and almost a quarter had posts frozen in the past year. NHS England figures for August 2026 showed more than 86,000 people waiting for a first community speech and language therapy appointment.
items.why: Staff shortages and frozen posts can lengthen waits for assessment, therapy and AAC support for children who are pre-verbal and non-verbal.

items.title: Speech and Language UK warns the oracy push could leave some pupils behind
items.summary: Writing in Tes, Speech and Language UK's director of policy and evidence welcomed the Education Secretary's plan to give oracy equal status with reading and writing in the revised national curriculum, but argued it must be inclusive from the start. She called for teacher training on speech, language and communication, clear routes to specialist help, and progress measures that do not assume fluent speech, and said pupils who communicate through signing or assistive technology should be recognised as part of the oracy agenda.
items.why: How oracy is defined and assessed in the new curriculum will affect whether pre-verbal and non-verbal pupils who use signing or communication aids are treated as taking part.

items.title: DfE issues SEND improvement notices to St Helens and Cornwall
items.summary: The Department for Education published an improvement notice requiring St Helens Council to take set steps to improve its SEND services, following a June 2026 Ofsted and CQC area SEND inspection that identified two areas for priority action. A separate notice published the same day applies to Cornwall Council, whose May 2026 inspection found inconsistent experiences and outcomes for children with SEND.
items.why: Improvement notices put local SEND services under closer government oversight, which families in those areas can use to ask what is changing in assessment and therapy support.

items.title: Government pays 5.8 billion pounds to clear most council SEND deficits
items.summary: The Department for Education published allocations of its high needs stability grant, with about 5.8 billion pounds paid to 129 councils to cover 90% of SEND deficits built up to the end of 2025-26, leaving councils to manage the remaining 10%. Twelve councils, including Bradford, had not yet had their local SEND reform plans approved and so had not received the grant.
items.why: Councils still carrying deficits, or waiting for plan approval, may face tighter budgets for specialist services such as therapy and communication aids during the move to the new system.

items.title: Councils call for a long-term funding plan for the SEND reforms
items.summary: The f40 group of lower-funded councils warned that the SEND reforms risk falling short because schools and councils cannot yet see how the system will be funded beyond the first year of the inclusive mainstream fund. The Department for Education said the reforms are backed by 4 billion pounds and that it plans to move more SEND funding into core school budgets, though it has not yet responded to its funding consultations.
items.why: Schools planning inclusion strategies without multi-year budgets may be cautious about committing to staff training, therapy time or equipment for pupils who communicate without speech.

items.title: Budget confirms 90% reimbursement of past council SEND deficits as OBR warns of rising pressure
items.summary: Alongside the Budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility noted the government's commitment to reimburse councils for 90% of SEND deficits built up to the end of 2025-26, with no commitment yet for deficits after that. It forecasts council SEND deficits rising from 2.8 billion pounds in 2025-26 to 5.7 billion pounds in 2027-28, before central government takes over SEND funding from 2028-29.
items.why: Council budgets stay under strain until 2028, which can affect how quickly local areas fund therapy, communication aids and specialist support for pre-verbal and non-verbal children.

items.title: Local SEND Reform Plans begin reshaping services before the law changes
items.summary: Special Needs Jungle reviewed 60 of the more than 150 Local SEND Reform Plans that councils, health boards and parent carer forums prepared for the Department for Education, and found them very similar and clearer on aims than on who will deliver the work. The DfE says over 90% of plans have been approved, which is linked to a rebate of up to 90% of council deficits, and the plans include targets to reduce EHC needs assessment requests and specialist placements.
items.why: Local targets on therapist input at SEN Support and on fewer EHC needs assessments could change how children who communicate without speech are assessed and supported in their area.

items.title: CQC State of Care: more than 80,000 children wait over a year for community health care
items.source: Healthcare Management UK (reporting the CQC State of Care report)
items.summary: The Care Quality Commission's annual State of Care report found that more than 80,000 children and young people in England had waited over a year for community health appointments. Children were far more likely than adults to face year-long waits, with many waiting for autism and ADHD assessments.
items.why: Community services include speech and language therapy, so long waits can mean children who communicate without speech go without specialist input for a large part of their early years.

items.title: Early years results show a wide gap for children with SEND
items.summary: The Department for Education's 2025-26 Early Years Foundation Stage Profile results showed 72.3% of Reception pupils reached a good level of development, a record high. Among pupils with SEND the figure was 24.1%, compared with 80.5% for pupils without SEND.
items.why: Communication and language is one of the prime areas measured at age five, so the gap shows how early pre-verbal and non-verbal children fall behind the expected milestones.

items.title: Where the SEND reforms stand after the consultation
items.summary: The government has still not published its response to the SEND consultation that closed in May, though the Department for Education says it remains committed to the timetable set out in the February Schools White Paper. Lucy Powell is now Education Secretary, Georgia Gould still leads on SEND, and Individual Support Plans are planned from 2029 with no changes to EHCPs before at least September 2030.
items.why: Families and schools still do not know the final shape of plans and legal protections, so current EHCP rights and processes continue to apply for now.

items.title: Bradford opens its first centre to help children with complex SEND stay in school
items.summary: Bradford Council has opened the SCIL Centre at Margaret McMillan Primary School to support children with complex special educational needs from across the district. The council says it has already helped reduce permanent exclusions and will act as a training hub for school staff.
items.why: Bradford families of children with complex communication needs may see more specialist advice reach mainstream classrooms rather than relying on a move to another setting.

items.title: DfE surveys point to gaps in specialist support in mainstream schools
items.summary: Special Needs Jungle brought together recent Department for Education survey findings showing that a fifth of parents whose child with SEND needed speech and language therapy said it was not received. School leaders also reported shortages of teaching assistants, and many cited funding and local availability as barriers to using speech and language support staff.
items.why: The figures suggest therapy and in-class support for children who communicate without speech is still patchy, which matters as the reforms ask mainstream schools to do more.

items.title: First DfE SEND training for teachers includes a speech, language and communication module
items.summary: The first set of Department for Education SEND and inclusion training materials for schools, developed by Ambition Institute, covers inclusive teaching and a closer look at speech, language and communication development. Speech and Language UK welcomed the focus but criticised the absence of developmental language disorder and the lack of practical classroom strategies.
items.why: Teachers will be expected to understand communication development, which could shape how classrooms respond to pupils who are pre-verbal and non-verbal.

items.title: Petition to keep SEND legal rights passes 100,000 signatures
items.summary: A parliamentary petition calling on the government to keep existing SEND legal rights passed 100,000 signatures on 30 September, the level at which Parliament considers a debate. The petition was started by a 15-year-old autistic campaigner and is supported by the Save Our Children's Rights coalition.
items.why: The scale of the response shows how concerned many families are about future entitlements, and a debate could put questions about EHCP protections on the parliamentary record.

items.title: RCSLT Bulletin focuses on AAC for its autumn issue
items.source: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists
items.summary: The autumn issue of the RCSLT Bulletin marks AAC Awareness Month with a focus on augmentative and alternative communication services. Its cover feature looks at progress and obstacles for children who need AAC, including common myths and practical tips.
items.why: It gives therapists and families current professional thinking on AAC for children, including the misconceptions that can delay a child being offered a communication aid.

items.title: Speech and language therapists press for investment ahead of the Budget
items.source: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists
items.summary: The RCSLT's Invest in SLT campaign is asking supporters to email the Prime Minister to make speech and language therapy a priority in the 28 October Budget. Earlier in September the college backed a Health Bill amendment that would require a strategy on access, waiting times and the workforce.
items.why: Funding and workforce decisions in the Budget will affect how quickly children who communicate without speech can be assessed and supported by a therapist.

items.title: Communication Matters holds its international AAC conference in Leeds
items.summary: The Communication Matters International AAC Conference took place at the University of Leeds from 13 to 15 September 2026, followed by an AAC study day on 16 September. The event brings together AAC users, families, therapists, educators and researchers, and this year coincided with the charity's 40th anniversary.
items.why: The UK's main AAC gathering being held in West Yorkshire gave local families and professionals direct access to current practice and research on communication aids.

items.title: SEND tribunal appeals reach a record quarterly high
items.summary: Official tribunal statistics show 8,800 SEND appeals were registered between April and June 2026, the highest quarterly figure on record and 22% more than a year earlier. The open caseload rose to 18,000, and most listed SEND hearings in 2025-26 were postponed.
items.why: Families who disagree with a council decision on an EHCP face longer waits for a hearing, which can delay agreed provision such as therapy or communication support.

items.title: Councils warn of recruitment risks to the Experts at Hand plan
items.summary: Draft SEND reform plans submitted by councils to the Department for Education flag difficulty recruiting speech and language therapists, educational psychologists and occupational therapists for the 1.8 billion pound Experts at Hand scheme. Some councils also raised concerns about one-year funding and a possible rise in EHCP requests during the transition.
items.why: If therapist posts cannot be filled, the promised local bank of specialists may reach schools slowly, affecting children who rely on therapy to develop their communication.

items.title: Solihull area SEND inspection published
items.summary: Ofsted and the CQC graded the Solihull local area partnership in the middle of their three-point scale after an inspection in July 2026. Inspectors praised multi-agency working and support for speech and language needs, but said the quality of EHC plans, preparation for adulthood and health assessment waits needed to improve.
items.why: Area inspections are now looking at speech and language support as part of judging local SEND services, which gives families a public measure of how well their area is doing.
